questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I found that the University I chose had the most interesting subjects of all the places I looked into. Furthermore, I really wanted to live in Australia, so that was a part of my decision as well.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I loved studying abroad, and can recommend it to anyone! I will say though, that it was expensive, and getting funding is not as easy as one might think. I applied for approximately 20 grants and got none of them (might be a me problem, who knows, but it's worth taking into account).

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was okay, the University of Melbournes website is a bit confusing, and there's too many portals to navigate in. But once you know where to look, information is easily acquired.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: The University provided free transportation from the airport upon arrival. You have to order it by email some time in advance, but they drive you all the way to your destination, and you get to meet some other students at the airport which is nice after a long journey.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was surprisingly easy to find somewhere to live. I know that some of my peers didn't have the same experience as me, but I found a lovely place to stay through a Facebook group (Fairy Floss Melbourne) where there's listings of rentals all the time. I lived in a share house, which is very normal in Melbourne, and had 2 roommates.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I can thoroughly reccomend finding housing off campus - cheaper, and a more fun and local experience! My experience is that you get more in touch with the neighborhoods and get a greater chance on meeting locals. Almost all my friends were locals, and I'm really happy that I then have some friends to go back to :)

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I almost gave up applying to University of Melbourne, simply because it is so confusing to find the right place for courses and subjects. First, be aware that their lingo is a bit different from the one most institutions use: If you register to a Course it's a degree (Bachelors or Masters Course), the chance is that you want to register into subjects. Knowing that, can save you a ton of time navigating their websites.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: Once you get the confirmation from your home institution, the University does provide you with some video guides on how to register. You register through a portal you probably will never use again. Watch the videos thoroughly, I found that it was a bit of a tedious process, but there is help, so don't wait with all the practicals, get started early on. This will also ease your mind when applying for your visa, as you will need the CoE from the university before you can do that :)

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: You could email the exchange student supervisors, but the University of Melbourne has a huge chunk of exchange students, and the reply time could sometimes reflect that. They do have a ton of video material to guide you, so that is a bonus!

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I did register into all of the classes I wanted, but only because I took my time getting to know the system of time slots and what nots. It can be a bit confusing to figure out if the classes are at the same time or if you can change the timeslots - sometimes you can, but it depends on the size of the subjects. I found that there was a lot of lectures offered in the faculty of Economics, but not at the faculty of arts.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: It is all worth the hassle.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was really good, my only hurdle is the amount of physical mandatory attendance they require. That takes a bit of getting used to.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I took both level 1, 2 and 3 subjects* (they are not called courses, at UniMelb). As a third year student, the level 1 subject was too easy and the level 3 subject was good! The level 1 subject was in the faculty of arts and the level 3 subject was in the faculty of law. My level 2 subjects were both in Econ, and they were challenging.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: There is mandatory tutorials each week for each study. The grading system is not only based on the exam but also on the tutorial attendance and assignments. There is many assignments, and the mandatory attendance was a stress factor, but the lectures were of such high quality!

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
1. Introductory Macroeconomics 
2. Globalization and the World economy
3. Global Environmental Politics 
4. Sustainability: Hope for the Earth?

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I really enjoyed Global Environmental Politics. The lecturer is so talented, and the big research essay we got to write (70% of the grade) taught me so much and was really fascinating. If you are interested in climate change and politics, I can't recommend this enough.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I had to go to the doctor a few times, and unfortunately also had to go with an ambulance once, and it is expensive. The insurance covers approximately half, but getting medical blood tests etc is very expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
Cafés and restaurants are cheaper than at home, and its great (and so tempting to spend a lot of money all the time). 
I also bought a bike from Facebook Marketplace and that was super cheap too.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They do a lot to tell the students in the intro week that there is a lot of clubs, and I signed up for like 4 of them but never heard anything. You have to very actively seek up the club opportunities. The Campus gym is cheap and good, and I used it a a lot ! There's also many coffee places at campus, but it is not student cheap per se.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They don't really host parties the same way as at KU, but the introduction week is really fun and they have a lot of shenanigans happening. It wasn't really clear if they offered any cultural events that wasn't students rallies (they have a lot of those) - it is a huge campus, and any event hosted by the institution can be a bit overwhelming.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Again, I would recommend their gym. It's cheaper than the local gyms, and its easy to go directly from lecture to the gym.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: I went to Phillip Islands, Great Ocean Road, Tasmania and New Zealand. It was all so so amazing, and I cannot recommend going on trips enough! My roommate had a car I could borrow and did often go on hikes in national parks with my friends - there is a lot of great hiking opportunities in and around Melbourne if your budget is not for the bigger trips.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: As I got an off campus housing situation, I got a lot of local friends which was really great for my feeling of belonging. There is a great culture for not gatekeeping your friend groups, so if you want to be a part of a friend group it is not impossible :)

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I only have 2 friends from campus, they were both exchange students and we met at an exchange party. It is hard to get friends from campus, but try to connect with someone you like at the tutorials.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: There isn't many, but the biggest one is that they are way younger at the universities in Australia versus here. I'm 27 and most people I met was 18-20 ish. It's not bad, but it could be a little alienating to be that much older.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People are open and easy to talk to!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Buy a bike (and don't be scared to ride it on the left side!)

Get an opportunity to buy/rent/borrow a car once in a while to get out of the city hustle. Trust me, you'll need it. 

Take your time deciding on the right subjects - they have so many but don't let that overwhelm you, if you do your research you will get an opportunity to study such interesting subjects!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Can't think of any

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The trips I took to the nature sites. It was so amazing to be in such different environments, and go explore all the opportunities to see the Australian wild.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Loneliness and anxiety was a big one for me, but the institution provide free professional counseling if you ever feel overwhelmed or alone. I used 4 out of six sessions, and helped me a lot. I know some other students who did the same, and it is really helpful.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: This is a long survey :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
